<reason>While Side B built an intuitive and well-written case around how shrinkflation exploits familiar packaging, Side A won by exposing a fatal contradiction at the heart of B's mechanism. Side B argued that existing unit prices across the shelf and on apps are tiny, inconsistent, and "designed to be missed," yet simultaneously claimed that slapping a prominent warning badge only on a downsized £2.00 item would not steer shoppers toward costlier rivals because shoppers would compare its £1.11/100g unit price against the rival's £1.25/100g—which remains buried in that same unread, inconsistent fine print. Side A also cleanly dismantled B's logistics defense regarding food apps (pointing out that customers view app pages before workers pick from mixed stock) and credibly established the perverse incentive toward unflagged ingredient dilution.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side A's pincher move in [A4.2]-[A4.3] and [A5.2]-[A5.3], using Side B's own premise that rival unit prices are buried in "tiny, inconsistent print" or hidden behind app taps to prove that an asymmetric warning badge on a downsized product will distort cross-brand comparisons rather than clarify them.</best_rebuttal>
